title: Why Intel’s EMIB Matters for Microsoft Azure
gist: Microsoft is the first company to announce plans to use Intel Foundry's EMIB packaging for its own Azure silicon, as part of an expanded multiyear Microsoft-Intel deal that also secures Xeon (Diamond Rapids) supply and collaboration on CXL memory, QuickAssist and confidential-VM migration; Nenni argues EMIB lets Azure co-design die-to-die connections with workloads, though no specific services or gains have been disclosed.

insights.claim: Microsoft is the first company to announce plans to use Intel Foundry's Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge (EMIB) packaging for silicon it designs for Azure, under an expanded multiyear Microsoft-Intel agreement.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Puts Intel Foundry's advanced packaging on a major hyperscaler's custom-silicon roadmap, a credibility win for Intel's foundry business.

insights.claim: For Intel Foundry, Microsoft's announcement places EMIB on the roadmap of a major cloud provider's in-house silicon program, which may be the most consequential part of the broader deal.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Packaging may be Intel Foundry's earliest monetizable wedge with hyperscalers, ahead of leading-edge wafer wins.
insights.quote: the most consequential part of the multiyear agreement may be how Microsoft puts its future Azure chips together

insights.claim: Microsoft and Intel have not yet detailed which Azure services will use EMIB-packaged silicon or what performance gains customers should expect.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The deal is a roadmap commitment, not yet a quantified volume win; wait for product and volume disclosures before sizing revenue impact.

insights.claim: EMIB uses a small bridge embedded in the package to give separate dies a short, dense connection, letting engineers decide which functions to integrate, which to develop separately, and how much bandwidth each link needs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Bridge-based packaging enables disaggregated, workload-tuned chip designs, a key enabler of hyperscaler custom silicon.

insights.claim: Because AI services are often bottlenecked on moving data between memory and compute, packaging control lets Microsoft devote more resources to data movement where bandwidth is the constraint, designing inter-component connections as deliberately as the components.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis that advanced packaging, not just process node, drives AI infrastructure performance.
insights.quote: The opportunity is to design the connections between components as deliberately as the components themselves.
insights.locator: That flexibility matters because cloud workloads

insights.claim: Splitting designs into dies lets Azure engineers revise one die as workload requirements change while carrying forward others, giving a longer-term design-iteration advantage.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Chiplet-based custom silicon can lower redesign cost and speed generational updates for hyperscalers.
insights.locator: There’s also a longer-term design advantage

insights.claim: The expanded Microsoft-Intel agreement secures multiyear supply capacity for Intel Xeon processors for Azure, including the next-generation Diamond Rapids family.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Multiyear Xeon commitments support Intel's data-center CPU volume visibility amid competitive pressure.

insights.claim: Microsoft and Intel are also collaborating on more flexible server memory via Compute Express Link, faster SQL backups using Intel QuickAssist Technology, and migrating confidential virtual machines between hosts with memory and processor state kept encrypted.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: CXL and confidential-computing collaboration deepens platform lock-in for Intel in Azure beyond raw CPU supply.
